title: Topic Drill: Data, Probability and Statistics (Set B)

items.stem: Five teams reach the final round of a robotics competition. In how many different ways can first, second and third place be awarded?
items.explanation: Order matters for places, so use a permutation: 5 choices for first, 4 for second and 3 for third, and 5 times 4 times 3 is 60. The value 10 is the number of groups of three teams, which ignores order. The value 15 multiplies 5 by 3 only. The value 125 lets one team win more than one place, 5 times 5 times 5.

items.stem: An observatory records the number of meteors seen each night for two weeks. A volunteer later adds 5 to every value in the data set to correct a counting offset. What happens to the mean and the standard deviation?
options: Both the mean and the standard deviation increase by 5.
The mean stays the same, and the standard deviation increases by 5.
Both the mean and the standard deviation stay the same.
The mean increases by 5, and the standard deviation stays the same.
items.explanation: Adding the same number to every value shifts the whole set up without changing the gaps between values, so the mean rises by 5 while the spread, and so the standard deviation, is unchanged. Claiming that both rise treats spread as if it moved with the center. Claiming the mean stays put ignores that every value went up. Multiplying, not adding, would change the spread.

items.stem: A library has 6 new books and will choose 3 of them for a front display, with no particular order on the shelf. How many different sets of 3 books can be chosen?
items.explanation: Order does not matter for a set, so use a combination: 6 times 5 times 4 is 120 ordered picks, and dividing by the 6 orders of the same three books gives 20. The value 120 skips that division. The value 18 multiplies 6 by 3. The value 216 allows repeated books, 6 times 6 times 6.

items.stem:
A river cleanup logged whether crews collected bags of trash. Some cells are missing.

Crew | Collected bags | Did not collect | Total
Morning | 28 | ? | 40
Afternoon | ? | 9 | 35
Total | ? | ? | 75

In all, how many volunteers did not collect bags?
items.explanation: The morning crew has 40 minus 28, or 12, who did not collect bags. Adding the afternoon crew’s 9 gives 12 plus 9, or 21 in all. The value 12 counts only the morning crew, and 9 counts only the afternoon crew. The value 54 is the number who did collect bags, 28 plus 26, which answers the opposite question.

items.stem: A night-sky observatory plotted each night’s hours of cloud cover against the number of stars catalogued. The points cluster tightly around a line that slopes downward from left to right. How would you describe the correlation?
options: Strong negative
Strong positive linear
Weak positive association
No correlation at all
items.explanation: When one variable rises as the other falls, the correlation is negative, and points hugging a line make it strong. So more cloud hours go with fewer stars catalogued. A positive label would need an upward slope, which is the most common sign slip. No correlation needs a shapeless cloud of points, not a tight band that follows a clear downward direction.

items.stem: A wetland survey asked 50 volunteers what they saw: 30 saw herons, 25 saw egrets, and 10 saw both. If one volunteer is chosen at random, what is the probability that this volunteer saw a heron or an egret?
items.explanation: Volunteers who saw at least one bird number 30 plus 25 minus 10, or 45, since the 10 who saw both were counted twice. Then 45/50 reduces to 9/10. The value 1/5 is only the chance of seeing both, 10 of 50. The value 3/5 is the heron chance alone. The value 4/5 adds only the heron group and the overlap, 40 of 50.

items.stem: A robotics team’s line of best fit is y = 2.5x + 12, where x is practice hours per week and y is the predicted score. What score does the line predict for 8 practice hours per week?
items.explanation: Substitute 8 for x: 2.5 times 8 is 20, and adding 12 gives 32. The value 20 forgets the intercept of 12. The value 14.5 adds 2.5 and 12 without multiplying by 8. The value 96 multiplies 12 by 8, swapping the roles of the slope and the intercept. Checking order of operations keeps multiplication before addition.

items.stem: A bakery records the number of orders on 12 days, listed in order: 4, 6, 7, 9, 10, 12, 13, 15, 18, 20, 21, 25. Using the medians of the lower and upper halves as the quartiles, what is the interquartile range?
items.explanation: The lower half is 4, 6, 7, 9, 10, 12, with a median of 8 between 7 and 9. The upper half is 13, 15, 18, 20, 21, 25, with a median of 19. Then 19 minus 8 is 11. The value 21 is the full range, 25 minus 4. The value 12.5 is the median of the whole list. The value 9 subtracts the wrong pair, 18 minus 9.

items.stem: A school garden club fits the line of best fit y = 3x + 8 to its data, where x is the number of weeks since planting and y is a seedling’s height in centimeters. What does the slope, 3, tell you?
options: The seedling is predicted to be 3 centimeters tall at planting.
The seedling is predicted to be 8 centimeters tall after 3 weeks.
The seedling is predicted to grow about 8 centimeters each week.
The seedling is predicted to grow about 3 centimeters each week.
items.explanation: The slope is the change in y for each increase of 1 in x, so each week adds about 3 centimeters. The starting height at planting is the intercept, 8, not 3, which is why the first wrong choice swaps the two numbers. After 3 weeks the line gives 3 times 3 plus 8, or 17 centimeters. Growth of 8 per week confuses the intercept for the slope.

items.stem:
A transit rider poll of 180 people gave this two-way table.

Rider type | Prefers bus | Prefers train
Student | 36 | 24
Adult | 54 | 66

What percent of all riders surveyed are students who prefer the bus?
items.explanation: The cell for students who prefer the bus holds 36 riders, and the whole table has 180, so 36 divided by 180 is 20%. The value 60% is 36 out of the 60 students, a share within one row. The value 40% is 36 out of the 90 bus fans, a share within one column. The value 30% is the adult bus cell, 54 of 180.

items.stem: Scores at a robotics competition have this five-number summary: minimum 12, first quartile 20, median 26, third quartile 34, maximum 50. What is the interquartile range?
items.explanation: The interquartile range is the third quartile minus the first quartile: 34 minus 20 is 14. The value 38 is the full range, 50 minus 12. The value 22 subtracts the minimum from the third quartile, 34 minus 12. The value 8 is the gap from the median to the third quartile, 34 minus 26, which covers only part of the middle half.

items.stem: A transit planner stands at the central station and surveys every tenth rider who boards, starting from a randomly chosen rider. Which sampling method is this?
options: Systematic sampling
Stratified random sampling
Cluster sampling of stations
Convenience sampling
items.explanation: Picking every tenth member from an ordered flow, after a random start, is systematic sampling. Stratified sampling first splits the population into groups and samples from each. Cluster sampling picks whole groups and surveys everyone in them. Convenience sampling takes whoever is easiest to reach, which does not describe a fixed, repeated interval with a random start.

items.stem: A town library wants feedback from its patrons about its new evening hours, and the staff are drafting a short survey. Which survey question is least likely to bias the answers?
options: Don’t you agree that the wonderful new evening hours are a big improvement?
Wouldn’t extended hours obviously be better for everyone in town?
Surely you support the longer evening schedule, don’t you?
How do you feel about the library’s new evening hours?
items.explanation: A neutral question names the topic and invites any answer without pushing a view. The other questions use loaded words such as wonderful and obviously, or a tag such as don’t you, which nudge people toward agreeing. Bias in wording changes the results even when the sample itself is chosen fairly, so neutral phrasing matters.

items.stem: A library desk logged books returned each hour. The stem-and-leaf plot reads: stem 1, leaves 2 5 8; stem 2, leaves 0 1 1 4 7; stem 3, leaves 3 6 9; stem 4, leaf 5. For how many hours were at least 30 books returned?
items.explanation: Read each value as stem and leaf: the hours at 30 or more are 33, 36, 39 and 45, which is 4 hours. The value 5 wrongly includes 27, which is below 30. The value 8 counts the hours with fewer than 30 books, 12 minus 4. The value 2 counts the stems 3 and 4 instead of counting the leaves on them.

items.stem: A river cleanup has 300 volunteers: 180 adults and 120 youths. Organizers want a stratified sample of 50 volunteers that keeps the same proportions as the whole group. How many adults should be in the sample?
items.explanation: Adults make up 180 out of 300, which is 60%, and 60% of 50 is 30 adults. The value 20 is the number of youths, 40% of 50. The value 25 splits the sample evenly even though the groups are unequal. The value 18 divides 180 by 10, a shortcut that ignores the sample size of 50.

items.stem: A transit poll sampled 200 riders, and 40 of them said they prefer app tickets. The transit system has 6,000 riders. Based on the sample, about how many of all riders prefer app tickets?
items.explanation: The sample rate is 40 out of 200, or 20%, and 20% of 6,000 riders is 1,200. The value 240 adds 40 and 200, which does not scale a rate. The value 30 divides 6,000 by 200 and stops. The value 30,000 inverts the ratio, using 200 over 40 times 6,000, which produces more riders than the system has.

items.stem:
A regional bakery compared what customers bought.

Day | Bought bread | Pastry only
Weekday | 45 | 15
Weekend | 40 | 40

Which conclusion is best supported by the table?
options: A greater share of weekday customers bought bread, 75% compared with 50%.
Weekend customers were more likely to buy bread because that row has more customers.
The two days had the same bread rate because 45 is close to 40.
Only 45% of weekday customers bought bread, so pastry was more popular.
items.explanation: Compare rates within each row: weekday bread is 45 of 60, which is 75%, and weekend bread is 40 of 80, which is 50%. A bigger row total does not make bread more likely. Counts of 45 and 40 being close hides the different row sizes. The claim of 45% mistakes the count 45 for a percent, when the weekday share is really 75%.

items.stem: A transit poll reports that 58% of riders prefer evening trains, with a margin of error of plus or minus 4 percentage points. Which interval is the most reasonable range for the true percent in the whole rider population?
items.explanation: Subtract and add the margin to the estimate: 58 minus 4 is 54, and 58 plus 4 is 62. The range 58% to 62% only adds the margin and leaves out the lower side. The range 50% to 66% doubles the margin to 8 points. The range 4% to 58% treats the margin as a lower limit, which is a misreading of what the margin means.

items.stem: A regional bakery summarizes daily loaf sales in a box plot: minimum 40, first quartile 55, median 62, third quartile 80, maximum 120. Which statement does the box plot support?
options: On about one quarter of the days, the bakery sold more than 80 loaves.
On about half of the days, the bakery sold more than 80 loaves.
On only one day, the bakery sold more than 80 loaves.
On about three quarters of the days, the bakery sold fewer than 62 loaves.
items.explanation: The third quartile marks the point with 25% of the data above it, so about a quarter of the days topped 80 loaves. Half of the days lie above the median, 62, not above 80. Nothing says only one day exceeded 80, because the whisker reaching 120 can cover several days. The median 62 has half the days below it, not three quarters.

items.stem: At a regional bakery, 60% of customers buy bread, and 24% of customers buy both bread and honey. Of the customers who buy bread, what fraction also buy honey, written as a decimal?
items.explanation: A conditional probability divides the joint chance by the chance of the given event: 0.24 divided by 0.6 is 0.4. The value 0.24 is the joint chance, not conditioned on bread. The value 0.36 subtracts the two percents, 0.6 minus 0.24, which has no meaning here. The value 0.6 is simply the chance of buying bread.

items.stem: An observatory’s line of best fit predicts 56 stars for a certain night. The actual count that night was 62 stars. What is the residual, defined as actual value minus predicted value?
items.explanation: A residual is actual minus predicted, so 62 minus 56 is 6, and the point sits above the line. The value -6 reverses the subtraction, a common sign mistake. The values 56 and 62 only restate the predicted and actual counts, and neither one measures the gap between them. A positive residual means the line underestimated that night.

items.stem: The number of loaves in each order at a regional bakery is shown in a histogram with a long tail stretching to the right, since a few catering orders are very large. Which statement is most likely true?
options: The median is clearly greater than the mean.
The mean and the median are exactly equal to each other.
The mean cannot be found when the data are skewed.
The mean is greater than the median.
items.explanation: A tail on the right pulls the mean toward the large values, while the median resists extreme values, so the mean exceeds the median. The reverse describes a left tail. Equal values suit a symmetric shape, not this one. The mean can be calculated for any numeric data, so the last claim is incorrect, even if it is less typical.

items.stem: A seed packet in the school garden claims 80% of seeds will sprout. A student plants 50 seeds and 37 sprout. What is the experimental probability that a seed sprouts?
items.explanation: Experimental probability uses the observed results: 37 sprouts out of 50 seeds is 37/50, or 74%. The value 80% is the packet’s claimed, or theoretical, rate. The value 26% is the share that did not sprout, 13 of 50. The value 63% subtracts 37 from 100 as if 37 were already a percent, but the test used only 50 seeds.

items.stem: A school garden dot plot shows tomatoes picked from 20 plants. The dots at 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 tomatoes number 2, 3, 6, 5, 2 and 2. What percent of the plants produced more than 3 tomatoes?
items.explanation: Plants with more than 3 tomatoes are those at 4, 5 and 6: 5 plus 2 plus 2 is 9 plants. Nine out of 20 is 45%. The value 55% counts 3 tomatoes or fewer, 11 plants. The value 30% uses only the tallest column, 6 of 20. The value 20% counts only the plants at 5 and 6 tomatoes, 4 of 20.

items.stem: A wetland team numbers its 80 ponds and uses a random number list to choose 12 of them for water clarity tests. To which group can the team reasonably apply its results?
options: Only the 12 ponds that were tested.
All 80 ponds in the wetland, because the sample was chosen at random.
Ponds in other regions of the country.
No group at all, because only a small part of the ponds was tested.
items.explanation: A random sample of a population supports conclusions about that population, here all 80 ponds, with some uncertainty. Limiting the results to the 12 tested ponds ignores the purpose of sampling. Ponds in other regions were never in the population being sampled. A small random sample is still useful, so refusing to generalize is too cautious.

items.stem: A river cleanup needs 2 boat leaders chosen from 5 volunteers and 1 shore leader chosen from 3 other volunteers. How many different leader teams are possible?
items.explanation: Choose the boat leaders as a combination: 5 times 4 divided by 2 gives 10 pairs. Multiply by the 3 shore choices, and 10 times 3 is 30. The value 60 treats the two boat leaders as ordered, 5 times 4 times 3. The value 15 picks only one boat leader, 5 times 3. The value 13 adds 10 and 3 when the choices happen together and should be multiplied.

items.stem: In a school garden, Set P holds the plant heights 20, 21, 20, 19, 20 and Set Q holds 5, 35, 20, 10, 30, in centimeters. Both sets have a mean of 20. Without computing, which set has the greater standard deviation?
options: Set P, because it contains a repeated value.
Neither, because the two means are equal.
Set P, because its values are closer to the mean.
Set Q, because its values lie farther from the mean on average.
items.explanation: Standard deviation measures how far values typically sit from the mean. Set Q ranges from 5 to 35, far from 20, while Set P stays within 1 centimeter of 20. Equal means do not mean equal spread, which is why the tie claim fails. Closeness to the mean produces a smaller deviation, so it would make Set P the less spread out set, not the more.

items.stem: A garden club measured plant growth each week from week 2 to week 10 and found a strong linear trend. A member uses the line of best fit to predict height at week 60. How reliable is this prediction?
options: Reliable, because a straight line continues forever.
Unreliable, because week 60 lies far outside the weeks that were measured.
Reliable, because a strong correlation guarantees accuracy anywhere.
Unreliable, because predictions work only at weeks that were measured.
items.explanation: Predicting far beyond the data is extrapolation, and growth rarely stays linear for 50 extra weeks, so the result is shaky. Plants level off, so assuming the line goes on forever is the main error. A strong correlation describes the measured range only. Predictions between measured weeks, such as week 5, are fine, so the last choice is too strict.

items.stem:
A library desk tallied what visitors borrowed.

Visitor | Fiction | Nonfiction | Neither
Teen | 24 | 10 | 6
Adult | 20 | 25 | 15

Of the visitors who borrowed nonfiction, what fraction were teens?
items.explanation: Nonfiction borrowers total 10 teens plus 25 adults, which is 35. Teens make up 10 of them, so the fraction is 10/35, or 2/7. The value 1/4 divides by the 40 teens instead, reversing the condition. The value 1/10 divides by all 100 visitors. The value 5/7 is the adult share of the nonfiction group, not the teen share.

items.stem: A wetland survey counted frogs heard at 20 sites. A histogram groups the sites by frog count: 0 to 4 frogs, 2 sites; 5 to 9 frogs, 6 sites; 10 to 14 frogs, 7 sites; 15 to 19 frogs, 4 sites; 20 to 24 frogs, 1 site. What percent of the sites had at least 10 frogs?
items.explanation: Sites with at least 10 frogs are the last three bars: 7 plus 4 plus 1 is 12 sites. Twelve out of 20 is 60%. The value 40% counts the 8 sites with fewer than 10 frogs, the opposite group. The value 35% uses only the tallest bar, 7 of 20. The value 25% counts only the two highest bars, 5 of 20.

items.stem: At a school garden fair, a spinner has 5 equal sections, and 2 of them are blue. Over 20 spins, blue came up 10 times. Which statement is correct?
options: The theoretical probability of blue is 2/5, and the experimental probability is 1/2.
The theoretical probability of blue is 1/2, and the experimental probability is 2/5.
Both the theoretical and experimental probabilities of blue are 1/2.
The theoretical probability of blue is 2/5, and the experimental probability is 2/3.
items.explanation: Theoretical probability comes from the setup: 2 blue sections of 5 equal sections gives 2/5. Experimental probability comes from the trials: 10 blue results in 20 spins gives 1/2. The first wrong choice swaps the two labels. Matching both at 1/2 ignores the sections. The value 2/3 does not match any count in the problem.

items.stem: A regional bakery wants to know whether customers would like earlier opening hours. The owner asks only the people standing in the shop at 7 a.m. on weekdays. What is the main weakness of this survey?
options: The sample is too large to give a useful answer.
The question is certain to be a leading question.
A store can never use a random sample.
It leaves out customers who shop at other times, so the sample may not represent all customers.
items.explanation: The owner reached only early-morning weekday shoppers, who may want earlier hours more than evening or weekend customers do, so the results are biased. A large sample is not a flaw. Nothing in the stem shows the wording was leading. A shop can draw a random sample, for example from its loyalty list, so the last claim is simply false.

items.stem: An observatory club has 40 members. Of them, 24 enjoy studying planets, 18 enjoy studying galaxies, and 6 enjoy both. How many members enjoy neither?
items.explanation: Members who enjoy at least one topic number 24 plus 18 minus 6, or 36, because the 6 who enjoy both were counted twice. Then 40 minus 36 leaves 4 members. The value 2 is 24 plus 18 minus 40, which ignores the overlap. The value 16 is 40 minus 24, only removing the planet fans. The value 10 subtracts the overlap again, 40 minus 24 minus 6.

items.stem:
At a robotics competition, 40 rookie teams and 40 veteran teams were tracked.

Team type | Advanced | Did not advance
Rookie | 8 | 32
Veteran | 22 | 18

By how many percentage points was the veteran advance rate higher than the rookie advance rate?
options: 2.75 points
14 points
35 points
75 points
items.explanation: The rookie rate is 8 out of 40, or 20%, and the veteran rate is 22 out of 40, or 55%. The difference is 55 minus 20, or 35 percentage points. The value 14 subtracts counts, 22 minus 8, instead of rates. The value 2.75 is the ratio of the rates, not a difference. The value 75 adds the two rates together.

items.stem: At a robotics competition, Team Alpha’s score rose from 80 to 100, and Team Beta’s score rose from 50 to 65. Which statement is correct?
options: Team Alpha had the greater percent increase, because it gained 20 points to Beta’s 15.
Team Alpha had the greater percent increase, 25% compared with 15%.
The two teams had equal percent increases.
Team Beta had the greater percent increase, 30% compared with 25%.
items.explanation: Percent increase is the gain divided by the starting score. Alpha gained 20 on 80, which is 25%, and Beta gained 15 on 50, which is 30%. Comparing raw gains of 20 and 15 ignores the different starting points. The claim of 15% for Beta uses its gain as a percent. The scores did not rise by equal percents, because 25% and 30% differ.

items.stem: A town’s records show that months with more library visits also have more garden-seed sales, and the association is strong and positive. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: Library visits cause people to buy more garden seeds.
A third factor, such as the season, may influence both, so neither one necessarily causes the other.
Buying garden seeds causes people to visit the library more.
The pattern must be due to chance because it is so strong.
items.explanation: A strong association shows two measures move together, not that either one produces the other. A shared cause such as spring weather could raise both. The first two choices treat correlation as proof of cause, running the arrow in each direction. Calling a strong pattern chance gets it backward, since a tight pattern is less likely to be luck.

items.stem: Volunteer turnout at a river cleanup rose from 40% of invited neighbors to 60%. By what percent did the turnout rate increase relative to the earlier rate?
items.explanation: The rate rose from 40 to 60, a gain of 20 points. Relative to the earlier rate, that is 20 divided by 40, or 50%. The value 20% reports the gain in percentage points, not a percent change. The value 33% divides by the new rate, 60, instead of the old one. The value 150% mistakes the new rate for 150% of the old one when it is actually 60 over 40, plus the base.

items.stem: A transit rider poll recorded waiting times, in minutes, for 30 riders. A histogram shows 2 riders in 0 to 4, 8 in 5 to 9, 7 in 10 to 14, 9 in 15 to 19, and 4 in 20 to 24. In which interval does the median waiting time fall?
options: 5 to 9
items.explanation: With 30 riders, the median sits between the 15th and 16th values. Running totals are 2, 10, 17, so both the 15th and 16th riders are in the 10 to 14 bar. The 15 to 19 bar is the tallest, but the tallest bar marks the mode, not the middle. The 5 to 9 bar ends at the 10th rider, too early. The 20 to 24 bar holds only the top four riders.

items.stem:
During a wetland survey, volunteers logged each heron, egret and ibis seen on a visit.

Bird | Morning | Evening
Heron | 12 | 18
Egret | 15 | 30
Ibis | 13 | 12

One sighting is picked at random from the evening column. What is the probability that it is an egret?
items.explanation: The evening column totals 18 plus 30 plus 12, or 60 sightings, and 30 of them are egrets, so the chance is 30/60, which is 1/2. The value 3/10 divides egret evenings by all 100 sightings. The value 9/20 is the share of all sightings that are egrets, 45 of 100. The value 2/3 divides by the 45 egret sightings, reversing the condition.

items.stem: At a library reading challenge, 50 volunteers took a timed test, and Rafi’s speed is at the 80th percentile. About how many volunteers had a speed below Rafi’s?
items.explanation: The 80th percentile means about 80% of the group scored below him, and 80% of 50 is 40 volunteers. The value 10 is the number at or above his speed, the other 20%. The value 80 treats the percentile as a head count, though only 50 people took the test. The value 8 divides 80 by 10, a shortcut with no basis here.
